flashcards.q: List libuv's 6 event loop phases in order.
flashcards.a: Timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check (setImmediate), close callbacks.

flashcards.q: After every single callback returns, what two queues drain, in what priority order, before the loop proceeds?
flashcards.a: 1) process.nextTick queue fully (Node-specific, highest priority). 2) V8 microtask queue fully (Promise .then/.catch/.finally). Only then does the loop proceed to the next callback or phase.

flashcards.q: Is setTimeout(fn,0) vs setImmediate ordering deterministic? In what context is it guaranteed?
flashcards.a: Non-deterministic at a script's top level (depends on process startup timing). Guaranteed deterministic -- setImmediate always fires first -- when both are scheduled from inside an I/O callback, because CHECK (setImmediate) directly follows POLL, while TIMERS is the next loop iteration's first phase.

flashcards.q: What's the observable CPU signature of a synchronous CPU-heavy operation blocking Node's event loop, versus a blocking I/O call in FastAPI/WebFlux?
flashcards.a: Node CPU-blocking: CPU PEGGED near 100% on one core (genuinely computing). FastAPI/WebFlux blocking-I/O-call: CPU stays IDLE/low (blocked waiting on I/O, not computing) -- opposite signatures despite both collapsing throughput.

flashcards.q: What is libuv's thread pool for, and what's its default size?
flashcards.a: A small, fixed-size (default 4) pool of real background threads faking asynchrony for operations with no non-blocking OS syscall equivalent -- some fs operations, dns.lookup (not dns.resolve), some crypto (pbkdf2/scrypt). Must set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE before any thread-pool-using module first loads.

flashcards.q: Why is Node stream backpressure called 'cooperative, not enforced'?
flashcards.a: writable.write() returning false is only a REQUEST to pause -- nothing in the runtime forces the producer to stop. A producer ignoring it keeps succeeding (data keeps being buffered) until memory pressure becomes an incident -- the real Walmart production memory leak was exactly a missing backpressure check in Node core's own C++.

flashcards.q: What's the safe default for wiring a Node stream pipeline, and why?
flashcards.a: stream.pipeline() (from node:stream/promises) or .pipe() -- both respect backpressure automatically and handle error propagation/cleanup correctly by default, unlike hand-rolled 'data'/'drain' event wiring which is a well-documented source of real production memory leaks.

flashcards.q: What does @nestjs/platform-fastify solve, and what's NestJS's default adapter as of v11?
flashcards.a: NestJS v11 defaults to Express v5, whose overhead is real and measurable; the Fastify adapter swaps in Fastify's faster routing while keeping NestJS's decorator-based DI/module structure, recovering most of the throughput gap for teams that want both structure and performance.

flashcards.q: What did Node's 2026 release schedule change to?
flashcards.a: Moved from odd/even major-version LTS pattern to one major release per year, landing every April with LTS promotion every October, removing the odd/even distinction entirely starting with Node 27.

flashcards.q: What does 'Node is single-threaded' actually constrain, and what does it not constrain?
flashcards.a: Constrains CPU-bound parallelism within one process (genuinely simultaneous computation needs worker_threads or a separate process). Does NOT constrain I/O-bound concurrency -- libuv's event loop lets one thread juggle thousands of concurrent I/O-waiting connections cheaply, which is the entire reason Node was designed this way.
